claim: Under awareness, threat-related emotional information, such as an angry or fearful face, has perceptual advantages.
source: Under awareness, threat-related emotional information, such as an angry or fearful face, has not only perceptual advantages but also guides rapid actions such as eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on emotional information processing under awareness.

claim: Under awareness, threat-related emotional information guides rapid actions such as eye movements.
source: Under awareness, threat-related emotional information, such as an angry or fearful face, has not only perceptual advantages but also guides rapid actions such as eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on emotional information processing under awareness.

claim: Emotional information that is suppressed from awareness still confers perceptual and attentional benefits.
source: Emotional information that is suppressed from awareness still confers perceptual and attentional benefits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on suppressed emotional information.

claim: It is unknown whether suppressed emotional information can directly guide actions.
source: However, it is unknown whether suppressed emotional information can directly guide actions, or whether emotional information has to enter awareness to do so.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in existing knowledge, representing the research question of the study.

claim: Under successful suppression, gaze moved towards fearful faces.
source: Under successful suppression, as indicated by objective and subjective measures, gaze moved towards fearful faces, but away from angry faces.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Under successful suppression, gaze moved away from angry faces.
source: Under successful suppression, as indicated by objective and subjective measures, gaze moved towards fearful faces, but away from angry faces.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Threat-related emotional stimuli can guide eye movements in the absence of visual awareness.
source: Our findings reveal that: (1) threat-related emotional stimuli can guide eye movements in the absence of visual awareness
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Threat-related emotional face information guides distinct oculomotor actions depending on the type of threat conveyed by the emotional expression.
source: (2) threat-related emotional face information guides distinct oculomotor actions depending on the type of threat conveyed by the emotional expression.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data showing differential effects for fearful vs. angry faces.

claim: Emotional information enhances visual sensitivity.
source: Emotional information enhances visual sensitivity (Phelps et al., 2006; Fox et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Emotional information potentiates effects of attention on visual sensitivity.
source: potentiates effects of attention on visual sensitivity (Ferneyhough et al., 2013; Bocanegra and Zeelenberg, 2009; Bocanegra and Zeelenberg, 2011a; Bocanegra and Zeelenberg, 2011b; Ohman et al., 2001; Lundqvist and Ohman, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Emotional information potentiates effects of attention on appearance.
source: and on appearance (Barbot and Carrasco, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Emotional information gains preferential access to awareness.
source: and gains preferential access to awareness (Amting et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2007; Milders et al., 2006; Hedger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Eye movements towards emotional, especially threat-related stimuli, are facilitated.
source: Eye (Bannerman et al., 2009a; Bannerman et al., 2009b; Bannerman et al., 2010; Nummenmaa et al., 2009) - or pointing (Valk et al., 2015) movements towards emotional –especially threat-related stimuli– are facilitated
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Saccades away from emotional, especially threat-related stimuli, are delayed.
source: whereas saccades away from these are delayed (Belopolsky et al., 2011; Kissler and Keil, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: People's eyes are usually attracted more towards emotional than neutral faces.
source: Usually, people's eyes are attracted more towards emotional than neutral faces (Mogg et al., 2007; Kret et al., 2013a; Kret et al., 2013b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sometimes gaze is repelled from threat-related (angry or fearful) faces.
source: yet, sometimes gaze is repelled from threat-related –angry or fearful– faces (Hunnius et al., 2011; Becker and Detweiler-Bedell, 2009; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The recognition of a face's emotional expression does not require awareness of the face.
source: Remarkably, the recognition of a face's emotional expression does not require awareness of the face.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent citations to research on cortically blind individuals and neurologically intact observers.

claim: Cortically blind individuals are able to correctly 'guess' the emotions of faces they cannot see.
source: Cortically blind individuals are able to correctly 'guess' the emotions of faces they cannot see (de Gelder et al., 2005; de Gelder et al., 1999; Pegna et al., 2005; Tamietto et al., 2009; Bertini et al., 2013; Striemer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In neurologically intact observers, emotional (especially threat-related) information they remain entirely unaware of is prioritized over neutral information.
source: In neurologically intact observers, emotional — especially threat-related — information they remain entirely unaware of, is prioritized over neutral information (Hedger et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Unaware emotional information facilitates visual discrimination.
source: facilitates visual discrimination (Bertini et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Unaware emotional information alters subsequent perceptual and discrimination judgments differentially for the unseen emotion.
source: and alters subsequent perceptual (Almeida et al., 2013) and discrimination judgments differentially for the unseen emotion (Zhan and de Gelder, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Emotional stimuli observers are unaware of elicit physiological reactions, for example changes in skin conductance.
source: Emotional stimuli observers are unaware of also elicit physiological reactions, for example changes in skin conductance (Esteves et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Emotional stimuli observers are unaware of elicit facial muscle activity and pupil dilation.
source: facial muscle activity and pupil dilation (Tamietto et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Unaware emotional stimuli activate subcortical structures, for example the amygdala, pulvinar, basal ganglia and superior colliculus.
source: and activate subcortical structures, for example the amygdala, pulvinar, basal ganglia and superior colliculus (Tamietto and de Gelder, 2010; Jiang and He, 2006; Troiani et al., 2014; Troiani and Schultz, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Unaware emotional stimuli activate cortical structures.
source: as well as cortical structures (Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When observers saccade towards color patches to report a mask's color, saccades initiation is slower departing from masked angry faces than from masked happy faces.
source: Furthermore, suppressed emotional stimuli influence oculomotor response times; when observers saccade towards color patches to report a mask's color, saccades initiation is slower departing from masked angry faces than from masked happy faces (Terburg et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Eye movements and visual awareness for neutral stimuli can be dissociated.
source: Eye movements are the ideal testing ground for the relation between suppressed emotional information and actions, as recent evidence has shown that eye movements and visual awareness for neutral stimuli can be dissociated (Spering and Carrasco, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The dissociation of eye movements and visual awareness reflects situations in which the direction of eye movements change in response to particular visual features, even though observers are unable to report these features because they are not aware of them.
source: The dissociation of eye movements and visual awareness reflects situations in which the direction of eye movements change in response to particular visual features, such as orientation or motion direction, even though observers are unable to report these features because they are not aware of them (Spering and Carrasco, 2015; Spering and Carrasco, 2012; Spering et al., 2011; Rothkirch et al., 2012; Glasser and Tadin, 2014; Kuhn and Land, 2006; Simoncini et al., 2012; Tavassoli and Ringach, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Suppressed neutral stimuli determine the trajectory of eye movements in the absence of awareness.
source: In other words, suppressed neutral stimuli determine the trajectory of eye movements in the absence of awareness.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited research on dissociation of eye movements and awareness.

claim: Visual attention can modulate the processing of neutral stimuli and the eye movements they elicit even when observers are unaware of them.
source: Moreover, visual attention can modulate the processing of neutral stimuli and the eye movements they elicit even when observers are unaware of them (Spering and Carrasco, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Angry and fearful faces convey different types of threat.
source: Angry and fearful faces convey different types of threat, and elicit different reactions under awareness.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and subsequent citations.

claim: Fearful faces indicate a potential indirect threat in the environment of the fearful person without indicating the source of the threat.
source: Fearful faces indicate a potential indirect threat in the environment of the fearful person without indicating the source of the threat, suggesting more information is needed to appraise the situation (Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The ambiguity of fearful faces leads to increased amygdala activation.
source: This ambiguity leads to increased amygdala activation (Whalen et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Fearful faces heighten visual attention to the seen fearful stimulus location.
source: heightens visual attention to the seen fearful stimulus location (Phelps et al., 2006; Ferneyhough et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fearful faces attract eye movements that enable detailed processing of the face and its environment.
source: and attracts eye movements that enable detailed processing of the face and its environment (Mogg et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Angry faces indicate direct threats.
source: Angry faces indicate direct threats (a person with an angry expression looking directly at the observer) leading to avoidance (Schmidt et al., 2012; Marsh et al., 2005) or freezing (Roelofs et al., 2010) responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When looking at angry faces observers show a stronger startle reflex than when looking at fearful faces.
source: When looking at angry faces observers show a stronger startle reflex (Springer et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When looking at angry faces observers show stronger activation of the torso muscles than when looking at fearful faces.
source: stronger activation of the torso muscles (Huis In 't Veld et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When looking at angry faces observers show widening of the pupils compared to when looking at fearful faces.
source: widening of the pupils (Kret et al., 2013b)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When looking at angry faces observers show higher activation in brain areas associated with defense preparation than when looking at fearful faces.
source: and higher activation in brain areas associated with defense preparation (Williams et al., 2005; Pichon et al., 2009; Kret et al., 2011) than when looking at fearful faces.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Threat processing is considered to evolve along two distinctive neuronal pathways, a fast sub-cortical and a slower cortical route.
source: Threat processing is considered to evolve along two distinctive neuronal pathways, a fast sub-cortical and a slower cortical route (LeDoux, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Fear information, relative to anger information, may be preferentially processed along the fast, subcortical route.
source: There is some evidence that fear information, relative to anger information, may be preferentially processed along the fast, subcortical route (Luo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When observers are presented with unmasked angry and fearful faces, both attract or repel their attention and eye gaze equally strongly.
source: Yet, when observers are presented with unmasked angry and fearful faces, both attract (Mogg et al., 2007; Kret et al., 2013a) or repel (Hunnius et al., 2011; Becker and Detweiler-Bedell, 2009) their attention and eye gaze equally strongly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fearful faces have preferential access to awareness compared to neutral faces presented during continuous-flash suppression.
source: Fearful faces have preferential access to awareness (Yang et al., 2007; Milders et al., 2006; Troiani et al., 2014; Jusyte et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Angry faces remain suppressed longer than neutral faces presented during continuous-flash suppression.
source: whereas angry faces remain suppressed longer (Jusyte et al., 2015; Zhan et al., 2015), both compared to neutral faces presented during continuous-flash suppression (CFS).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Continuous flash suppression suppresses stimuli for up to several seconds.
source: In this way, continuous flash suppression suppresses stimuli for up to several seconds, enabling the measurement of eye movements in the absence of awareness (Rothkirch et al., 2012; Madipakkam et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: At ~400 ms after full display was reached, distance of gaze position to fearful faces decreased compared to neutral faces, indicating an orienting of gaze towards fearful faces.
source: At ~400 ms after full display was reached, distance of gaze position to fearful faces decreased compared to neutral faces, indicating an orienting of gaze towards fearful faces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Distance of gaze position to angry faces increased compared to the distance to neutral faces, indicating gaze aversion from angry faces.
source: In contrast, distance of gaze position to angry faces increased compared to the distance to neutral faces, indicating gaze aversion from angry faces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The pattern of differential eye movements for fearful and angry faces was not observed with upside-down presented faces.
source: This pattern of results was not observed with upside-down presented faces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The absence of an effect for upside-down presented faces rules out the possibility that low-level visual features were responsible for the effect observed with upright presented emotional faces.
source: The absence of an effect for upside-down presented faces rules out the possibility that low-level visual features were responsible for the effect observed with upright presented emotional faces, a confound not controlled for in previous studies (Bodenschatz et al., 2018) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing no effect for upside-down faces.

claim: Observers looked significantly longer towards the location at which an upright fearful face was displayed: dwell times at the target location increased by 57% compared to trials with upside-down presented fearful faces.
source: This dwell time analysis (Figure 4) showed that, observers looked significantly longer towards the location at which an upright fearful face was displayed: dwell times at the target location increased by 57% compared to trials with upside-down presented fearful faces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Observers looked significantly longer towards an adjacent location when an upright compared to an upside-down angry face was displayed, demonstrating a consistent and lasting gaze aversion from an angry face.
source: In contrast, observers looked significantly longer towards an adjacent location when an upright compared to an upside-down angry face was displayed, demonstrating a consistent and lasting gaze aversion from an angry face.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: No dwell time effect emerged for neutral faces.
source: No effect emerged for neutral faces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The objective performance measures validate the subjective visibility ratings.
source: Our objective performance measures (Figure 2, red dots) validate the subjective visibility ratings, and together indicate that the emotional faces were suppressed from perceptual awareness.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The emotional faces were suppressed from perceptual awareness.
source: Our objective performance measures (Figure 2, red dots) validate the subjective visibility ratings, and together indicate that the emotional faces were suppressed from perceptual awareness.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The absence of an effect with upside-down presented angry faces precludes confounds with low-level feature differences between faces of different emotional expressions.
source: The absence of an effect with upside-down presented angry faces precludes confounds with low-level feature differences between faces of different emotional expressions.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing no effect for upside-down faces.

claim: The elicited eye movements were specific to the displayed facial emotion regarding the type of threat it conveyed.
source: Remarkably, the elicited eye movements were specific to the displayed facial emotion regarding the type of threat it conveyed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing differential effects for fearful vs. angry faces.

claim: The distinct consequences on oculomotor actions demonstrate qualitative processing of the emotional expression, rather than mere detection of emotional stimuli in the absence of awareness.
source: These distinct consequences on oculomotor actions demonstrate qualitative processing of the emotional expression, rather than mere detection of emotional stimuli in the absence of awareness.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data showing differential effects for different emotions.

claim: For neutral stimuli, dissociations between visual awareness and eye movements have been related to the involvement of a fast subcortical retinocollicular pathway.
source: For neutral stimuli, dissociations between visual awareness and eye movements, revealing more sensitive processing of information, have been related to the involvement of a fast subcortical retinocollicular pathway (Spering and Carrasco, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Processing of unaware emotional visual information has been associated with a subcortical pathway involving the amygdala, pulvinar, and superior colliculus.
source: Furthermore, processing of unaware emotional visual information has been associated with a subcortical pathway involving the amygdala, pulvinar, and superior colliculus (Tamietto and de Gelder, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There are structural connections between the amygdala and cortical motor‐related areas.
source: as well as structural connections between the amygdala and cortical motor‐related areas (Grèzes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The superior colliculus plays a crucial role in the control of voluntary and involuntary eye movements.
source: The superior colliculus plays a crucial role in the control of voluntary and involuntary eye movements (Bell and Munoz, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of awareness, orienting of eye movements towards and away from emotional faces could be mediated by subcortical structures.
source: Thus, in the absence of awareness, orienting of eye movements towards and away from emotional faces could be mediated by these subcortical structures, in addition to the potential involvement of a cortical pathway (Pessoa and Adolphs, 2010).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from cited research and the current findings.

claim: A possible mechanism could be that the amygdala assesses facial emotional expression, and the superior colliculus guides eye movements according to a fight, flight, or freeze response.
source: A possible mechanism could be that the amygdala assesses facial emotional expression, and the superior colliculus guides eye movements according to a fight, flight, or freeze response.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism based on inference.

claim: Under awareness, angry and fearful faces have differential perceptual consequences.
source: As mentioned in the Introduction, under awareness these two threat-related emotions have differential perceptual consequences (Kret et al., 2013b; Marsh et al., 2005; Springer et al., 2007; Huis In 't Veld et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Angry and fearful faces may be mediated by different neural pathways.
source: and may be mediated by different neural pathways (Luo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of awareness, before this study, there had been only circumstantial evidence for differential processing of angry and fearful faces according to the time they take to break into awareness.
source: In the absence of awareness, before this study, there had been only circumstantial evidence for differential processing of angry and fearful faces according to the time they take to break into awareness (Yang et al., 2007; Milders et al., 2006; Troiani et al., 2014; Jusyte et al., 2015; Zhan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Under awareness, both angry and fearful faces have shown to elicit similar eye movement responses, either attraction or repulsion.
source: With respect to eye movements, under awareness, both angry and fearful faces have shown to elicit similar eye movement responses, either attraction (Mogg et al., 2007; Kret et al., 2013a) or repulsion (Hunnius et al., 2011; Becker and Detweiler-Bedell, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the absence of awareness, gaze avoidance from masked angry faces had been demonstrated only indirectly with eyes starting instructed movements towards a response target more slowly in the presence of an angry than a happy face.
source: In the absence of awareness, gaze avoidance from masked angry faces had been demonstrated only indirectly with eyes starting instructed movements towards a response target more slowly in the presence of an angry than a happy face (Terburg et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The current results show uninstructed, sustained gaze avoidance to an angry face but sustained gaze attraction to a fearful face, while the faces are entirely suppressed from awareness.
source: Instead, our results, directly measured with eye tracking, show uninstructed, sustained gaze avoidance to an angry face but sustained gaze attraction to a fearful face, while the faces are entirely suppressed from awareness.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the study.

claim: Directing our eyes towards fearful faces may be an automatic response to try to gather more information.
source: Fearful faces are more ambiguous and directing our eyes towards them may be an automatic response to try to gather more information (Bannerman et al., 2009a; Mogg et al., 2007; Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from cited research and the current findings.

claim: Directing our eyes away from angry faces may be an automatic avoidance response.
source: In contrast, angry faces pose a direct threat and directing our eyes away from them may be an automatic avoidance response (Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from cited research and the current findings.

claim: Comparing the finding of differential eye movements in the absence of awareness with previous findings of similar eye movements under awareness suggests that different factors may influence eye movements under aware and unaware conditions.
source: Comparing our finding of differential eye movements in the absence of awareness with the previous findings of similar eye movements under awareness (Mogg et al., 2007; Kret et al., 2013a; Hunnius et al., 2011; Becker and Detweiler-Bedell, 2009) suggest that different factors may influence eye movements under aware and unaware conditions.
evidence: This claim is an inference from comparing the current findings with prior research.

claim: Across studies, perceptual, attentional and physiological effects of emotional information either differ qualitatively or tend to be stronger in the absence than in the presence of awareness.
source: Across studies, perceptual (Lapate et al., 2016), attentional (Mogg et al., 1994; Fox, 1996) and physiological (Tamietto et al., 2015) effects of emotional information either differ qualitatively or tend to be stronger in the absence than in the presence of awareness (Diano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Awareness modulates the time course and locus of neural activations elicited by threat-related information.
source: Moreover, awareness modulates the time course (Liddell et al., 2004) and locus (Tamietto et al., 2015) of neural activations elicited by threat-related information
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Awareness modulates functional connectivity between the amygdala and pre-frontal areas.
source: as well as functional connectivity between the amygdala and pre-frontal areas (Amting et al., 2010; Lapate et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The perceived intensity of the threat might be stronger in the absence of awareness, which in turn may facilitate actions specifically tailored towards the nature of the threat.
source: Two different mechanisms might cause threat-related emotions guiding actions differentially in the absence, but not in the presence of awareness: a) the perceived intensity of the threat might be stronger in the absence of awareness (Lapate et al., 2016; Liddell et al., 2004), which in turn may facilitate actions specifically tailored towards the nature of the threat, indirect or direct
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism based on inference from cited research.

claim: Cognitive mechanisms might suppress automatic actions upon threat-related information only under awareness, but not in its absence.
source: b) cognitive mechanisms might suppress automatic actions upon threat-related information only under awareness (Whalen et al., 2013; Mogg et al., 1994), but not in its absence, as in our present findings.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism based on inference from cited research and the current findings.

claim: Several factors may help overwrite automatic eye movements towards fearful or away from angry faces, ranging from mere adherence to the task instructions to regulation of the social communication entailed in holding or averting gaze.
source: Several factors may help overwrite automatic eye movements towards fearful or away from angry faces, ranging from mere adherence to the task instructions (Becker and Detweiler-Bedell, 2009) to regulation of the social communication entailed in holding or averting gaze (Terburg et al., 2011; Emery, 2000; Kendon, 1967).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing possible factors based on inference from cited research.

claim: The results provide the first evidence that emotional information humans are unaware of can differentially modulate their eye movements without entering awareness.
source: To conclude, our results provide the first evidence that emotional information humans are unaware of can differentially modulate their eye movements without entering awareness.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the study.

claim: Twelve participants (four females, mean age 24.3 years) were included in the final analysis.
source: Twelve participants (four females, mean age 24.3 years) were included in the final analysis.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's sample.

claim: Emotional face stimuli were selected from 10 different identities (five male, five female) from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces database.
source: We selected emotional face stimuli (neutral, angry, and fearful expressions, all looking straight ahead) from 10 different identities (five male, five female) from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces database (Lundqvist et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's stimuli.

claim: With shorter presentation times emotion-specific effects are limited to upright presented faces.
source: The emotional expressions of upside down presented faces can elicit differential effects when these are presented for several seconds (McKelvie, 1995; Calvo and Nummenmaa, 2008; Derntl et al., 2009; Narme et al., 2011), but with shorter presentation times emotion-specific effects are limited to upright presented faces (Phelps et al., 2006; Bocanegra and Zeelenberg, 2009; Barbot and Carrasco, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mask images were displayed at a frequency of 28.3 Hz.
source: Mask images were displayed at a frequency of 28.3 Hz (Kaunitz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's methods.

claim: The flickering mask was always presented to the dominant eye and the low contrast face stimulus was presented to the non-dominant eye to achieve best possible suppression.
source: The flickering mask was always presented to the dominant eye (as determined with a hole-in-card test (Miles, 1930) at the start of the experiment for each participant) and the low contrast face stimulus was presented to the non-dominant eye to achieve best possible suppression.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's methods.

claim: The experiment comprised 288 trials divided into three blocks.
source: The experiment comprised 288 trials divided into three blocks to allow participants to rest and to re-calibrate the eye tracker.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's procedure.

claim: In 240 trials, the face stimulus was presented to the non-dominant eye and the flickering mask to the dominant eye to suppress the face image from visual awareness.
source: In 240 trials, the face stimulus was presented to the non-dominant eye and the flickering mask to the dominant eye to suppress the face image from visual awareness.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's procedure.

claim: The face stimulus was gradually faded in for 500 ms to make the suppression more effective.
source: Then the flickering mask appeared to the dominant eye, and the face stimulus, presented to the non-dominant eye, was gradually faded in for 500 ms, to make the suppression more effective (Tsuchiya et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study's procedure, supported by a citation.

claim: The suppressive effects of continuous flash suppression vary inter- and intra-individually.
source: The suppressive effects of continuous flash suppression vary inter- and intra-individually (Hesselmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the emotion task, participants were biased towards responding 'neutral' when they indicated that they had not seen the face.
source: In the emotion task, participants were biased towards responding 'neutral' when they indicated that they had not seen the face (while at the same time they were at chance level for the position task; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Two participants performed clearly above chance level (78% and 67% correct position responses) even though they indicated to not have seen the stimulus, and their data were excluded from all further analyses.
source: In the position task, two participants performed clearly above chance level (78% and 67% correct position responses) even though they indicated to not have seen the stimulus. Data from these two participants were excluded from all further analyses.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data exclusion criteria.
